summary: OpenManus funnels every LLM call through one place: app/llm.py builds a single AsyncOpenAI client per named config and ask(), ask_with_images() and ask_tool() all use it, so one wrap put all five production call sites on Router. The client now goes through router_runtime.wrap_openai(), which is inert until RAMP_ROUTER_API_KEY is set and keeps the app's own Chat Completions request shape, translating it to Router's /v1/responses. All four call shapes were exercised against the local simulator and against the real Router: plain chat, streaming chat, image input and a tool call that came back with the right function name, with token accounting and the existing retry behaviour unchanged. The two Bedrock calls stay on boto3 (Router does not serve the AWS converse endpoint with the shared key) and an api_type = "azure" deployment stays on Azure, as the runtime intends. Nothing else in the app talks to a model. On top of the migration I built two improvements: image input is restored for every current model by asking Router's catalog instead of a hard-coded 2024 list, and an operator can opt a non-OpenAI OpenAI-compatible host into Router, which matters because most OpenManus configs point base_url somewhere other than api.openai.com.
reviewed: I read the whole LLM layer (app/llm.py, app/bedrock.py, app/config.py and the shipped config examples) and measured the levers that looked promising for an agent loop rather than assuming them. Prompt caching turned out to need no new work: the migration already delivers it (measured 8,833 of 8,852 input tokens cached on a second agent-loop step on claude-haiku-5-5 via Router), and a router.policy.json prompt_cache_key added nothing on top, so I deleted that branch rather than ship a no-op. What did survive review were a correctness loss the migration exposes (a 2024 model list that blocks image input on every model Router serves), a coverage gap (only api.openai.com routes by default, while the shipped config examples point elsewhere), and two things I deliberately left as proposals because the right answer depends on the deployment's configured model and credentials: Router-side fallbacks and porting the Bedrock path.

items.title: Route the shared OpenAI client through Router
items.summary: Wrap the one AsyncOpenAI client app/llm.py builds so all five of its call sites reach Router when RAMP_ROUTER_API_KEY is set.
items.gains: One Router key and one spend view for every model call the app makes, with per-call spend labels (app/llm.py:ask, :ask_with_images, :ask_tool) and any catalog model reachable by changing config.llm.model alone. Prompt caching on Claude arrives with it: measured 8,833 of 8,852 input tokens cached on the second step of an agent loop, which is roughly -90% on the input cost of every step after the first, and that is the dominant cost in a ReAct loop that re-sends its whole history. Nothing changes until the key is set, and ROUTER_MIGRATE_DISABLE=1 turns it back off.
items.loses: The app always sends temperature for any model outside its REASONING_MODELS list, and 36 catalog ids reject temperature (Sonnet 5, every *-5-5, Opus 4.7 and later, the OpenAI reasoning models). On the Router path the runtime drops it rather than letting the call 400, so on those models config.llm.temperature stops having an effect instead of breaking the call. A translation layer also now sits in the request path: requests go out as Chat Completions and are converted to /v1/responses and back.
items.price: no change by itself; input cost per agent step drops about 90% once a step's prefix is cached
items.why: Every production call funnels through self.client in LLM.__init__, so one wrap at the construction covers ask(), ask_with_images() and ask_tool() including both their streaming and non-streaming branches. Wrapping under the client rather than pointing the client at Router keeps the app's own request shape, keeps the per-request provider fallback when Router refuses before generating, and leaves Azure and Bedrock deployments exactly where they were.

evidence.detail: compileall plus pytest tests/ --ignore=tests/sandbox: 4 passed, same as the baseline

check --run on a script driving the app's own LLM class: ask() non-streaming, ask() streaming, ask_with_images() and ask_tool() each produced one valid /v1/responses request, labelled app/llm.py:ask / :ask_with_images / :ask_tool; the tool call came back as function get_weather and token accounting logged normally
check --run --live with gpt-6-luna: 2 requests, both 200 from provider=openai, ask() returned text and ask_tool() returned the get_weather tool call

check --run --live with claude-haiku-5-5, two agent-loop-shaped calls sharing a ~8.8k-token prefix: step 2 read 8,833 of 8,852 input tokens from cache with the runtime's label-derived cache key, and 0 of 8,852 with ROUTER_MIGRATE_FEATURE_TAG=off; cache reads bill at the catalog's cache_read_input ($0.01 vs $0.10 per 1M on that model)

the temperature loss is real and benign: claude-haiku-5-5 has temperature: false in the catalog, and a live ask_with_images() call that sent temperature 0.0 returned 200 with the right answer, so the runtime did drop the field instead of 400ing
router-migrate check --all: 5 of 7 scanned calls route, the other 2 being the Bedrock pair in s1

items.title: Bedrock stays on boto3
items.summary: An api_type = "aws" deployment keeps calling Bedrock converse / converse_stream directly, because Router does not serve the AWS endpoint with the shared key.
items.gains: nothing changes for AWS deployments; the hand-written OpenAI-shaped adapter in app/bedrock.py keeps working as before
items.loses: an api_type = "aws" deployment gets none of Router's benefits: its spend is not in the Router view and it still needs its AWS credentials
items.why: app/bedrock.py speaks the boto3 bedrock-runtime converse protocol, which Router has no endpoint for, and the runtime deliberately leaves Bedrock clients alone. Reaching Router's Bedrock catalog ids means rewriting this client against Router's /v1/messages, which is the separate proposal i3 and still needs the caller's own AWS key because those ids are BYOK.

evidence.detail: router-migrate check --all reports both sites as kept: other SDK / endpoint

items.title: Azure deployments stay on Azure
items.summary: With api_type = "azure" the AsyncAzureOpenAI client is built on the other branch of the same if, and the runtime leaves Azure clients on their configured deployment.
items.gains: no behaviour change and no risk for Azure deployments
items.loses: an Azure deployment's traffic is not on Router, so its spend stays outside the Router view
items.why: Router serves OpenAI models under its own catalog ids, not through a customer's Azure deployment URL and deployment-name routing, so there is no safe automatic equivalent. Such a deployment would move by switching api_type away from azure and naming a catalog model, which changes which account is billed and is a deliberate operator decision, not a migration edit.

evidence.detail: app/llm.py:222-227 builds AsyncAzureOpenAI unwrapped; router_runtime.wrap_openai() returns Azure clients untouched by design

items.title: Take image support from Router's catalog
items.summary: Ask Router's catalog which models accept image input instead of matching against a hard-coded list of six models from early 2024.
items.gains: Restores image input on Router. MULTIMODAL_MODELS names gpt-4-vision-preview, gpt-4o, gpt-4o-mini and three claude-3 dated ids; Router serves none of the claude-3 or vision-preview ids, so on any current model ask_with_images() raised ValueError outright and ask()/ask_tool() silently deleted the base64_image off every message, which is how OpenManus's browser agent hands over screenshots. After the change a live claude-haiku-5-5 call read the image through both paths and answered correctly.
items.loses: Capability detection now depends on the catalog the vendored runtime carries, so a model added to Router after this runtime copy was vendored falls back to the old list until the runtime is refreshed. The Bedrock and Vertex BYOK ids are not in that vendored catalog either, so e.g. gemini-3.8-flash still reports no image support even though Gemini takes images. Both cases fail closed, the way the code behaved before.
items.price: no change per call; an agent step that now carries a screenshot costs that image's input tokens, which it was silently not sending before
items.why: The hard-coded list is the kind of thing Router makes unnecessary: the catalog already states input_modalities per model, and the vendored runtime carries that table, so the app can ask instead of guess. The guess was not merely conservative, it was wrong in the expensive direction, turning a vision-capable model into a text-only one with no log line, and turning the explicit ask_with_images() path into a hard error. The fall-back to the old list keeps behaviour identical for anything Router has no entry for, including the model = "test" the existing tests use.

evidence.detail: compileall plus pytest tests/ --ignore=tests/sandbox: 4 passed, unchanged; the image test in tests/tools/test_browser_use_mcp.py uses model = "test", which is not a catalog id, so it takes the unchanged fall-back path

the same probe on both branches with model claude-haiku-5-5: before, ask_with_images() raised ValueError and tenacity retried it to failure with 0 requests reaching Router; after, ask_with_images() and ask() with a base64_image each produced one valid Router request

check --run --live with claude-haiku-5-5 and a 128x128 red JPEG: 2 requests, both 200 from provider=anthropic, and the model answered "Red" through both ask_with_images() and ask() with base64_image, proving the image really reached it

model_supports_images now reports True for claude-sonnet-5, gpt-5.4, gpt-4o-mini and claude-3-opus-20240229, and False for deepseek-v4-flash (text-only in the catalog), gemini-3.8-flash (BYOK, not in the vendored catalog), "test" and llama3.2

items.title: Let an operator route another compatible host
items.summary: ROUTER_UNLOCK_HOSTS names OpenAI-compatible hosts other than api.openai.com whose catalog-model requests may go to Router.
items.gains: Makes the migration actually cover the way OpenManus is usually configured. The app points one OpenAI client at whatever base_url the config names, and the shipped examples use Anthropic's compatible endpoint (the default), Ollama, PPIO, Jiekou.AI and Google; only api.openai.com routes without this, so those deployments get nothing from m1. With the host listed, a request naming a Router catalog model goes to Router under the one key; the env var is unset by default, so nothing moves until an operator says so.
items.loses: Unlocking a host is a real decision, not a tidy-up: requests whose model is a catalog id stop reaching the endpoint the config names, so a deployment that deliberately pinned a vendor (or kept data inside its own network) would be sending those requests to Router instead, billed to the Router key and served by whichever provider Router picks. It also adds one more environment variable to get wrong. Requests naming a non-catalog model are unaffected, and an operator who sets nothing sees no change at all.
items.price: catalog list price on Router for the requests that move, instead of that vendor's own price, which may be higher or lower
items.why: The default host-locked behaviour is the right default but the wrong end state for this app, because its single client is a vendor-agnostic slot by design. Scoping the unlock to catalog ids is what makes it safe to offer: a self-hosted Ollama keeps serving llama3.2 locally even with its host unlocked, which I verified rather than assumed. Leaving it to an env var keeps the choice with whoever knows why that base_url was chosen.

evidence.detail: compileall plus pytest tests/ --ignore=tests/sandbox: 4 passed, unchanged

check --run on the default config shape (the OpenAI SDK pointed at https://api.anthropic.com/v1/ with claude-haiku-5-5): with ROUTER_UNLOCK_HOSTS unset the runtime kept every attempt on the vendor, with ROUTER_UNLOCK_HOSTS=api.anthropic.com it produced one valid Router request
the safety property holds: base_url http://localhost:11434/v1 with model llama3.2 and ROUTER_UNLOCK_HOSTS=localhost stayed on the provider, logged as model 'llama3.2' is not in the Router catalog

items.title: Port the Bedrock path onto Router's Messages API
items.summary: Proposal: replace app/bedrock.py's boto3 converse client with Router's /v1/messages, so AWS deployments land in the same spend view as everything else.
items.gains: One key and one spend view for api_type = "aws" deployments too, and roughly 330 lines of hand-written OpenAI-to-Bedrock message, tool and streaming translation replaced by a surface Router already serves. The Bedrock catalog ids the config would name (us.anthropic.claude-*, global.anthropic.claude-*, us.openai.gpt-*) are in Router's catalog, so the configured model string mostly survives the move.
items.loses: The AWS provider key is still required, because Router's Bedrock ids are BYOK, so this does not remove an AWS dependency. It is also a real rewrite of a working adapter: the streaming event shape, the tool-call assembly and the usage numbers would all come from a different protocol, and app/bedrock.py's OpenAI-shaped return objects would have to be rebuilt from Anthropic Messages responses. Anything the current adapter quietly tolerates could change behaviour, so it wants its own round of testing against a real AWS-backed key.
items.price: Router's catalog price for the Bedrock ids, which for the AWS-hosted Claude ids runs about 10% above the direct Anthropic ids (us.anthropic.claude-opus-5 $5.50/$27.50 against claude-opus-5 $5/$25)
items.why: Left for approval rather than built because the payoff depends on facts I cannot check from here: whether this deployment actually uses api_type = "aws", whether its AWS key is registered with Router for BYOK, and whether the model ids it names are the ones Router lists. If the answer to any of those is no, the rewrite is pure risk. If it uses AWS in production, this is the one remaining blind spot in the spend view and worth doing properly.

evidence.detail: nothing built; the Bedrock catalog ids and their BYOK requirement come from router-migrate levers and the fact sheet, and no AWS-backed credential was available to test a port

items.title: Add fallback candidates for the agent step
items.summary: Proposal: a router.policy.json fallbacks list for the app/llm.py:ask_tool label, so one refused step does not end a long agent run.
items.gains: An OpenManus run is a chain of ask_tool() steps and the agent aborts when one of them finally fails. Router's models list falls through a model the key may not use, a model that is missing and an invalid parameter without the app noticing, which turns several step-level failures into a slower but completed run. The policy applies only to Router-bound requests, so the provider path never sees the extra field.
items.loses: A different model can answer one step in the middle of a run, so a run's reasoning quality becomes uneven and harder to reproduce; the step is billed at whichever candidate served. Fallbacks also cancel the Flex discount on that label, and the weakest candidate caps what the request may ask for, which matters here because every ask_tool() call carries tool schemas. It does not help with the failures agent runs hit most often: Router's documentation says there is no fallback once a stream has started, and timeouts, 429 and 5xx go back to the app, where tenacity already retries them six times.
items.price: unchanged when the first candidate serves; the serving candidate's price otherwise
items.why: Left for approval because the candidate list cannot be written without knowing the deployment: the right second model for a gpt-5.1 deployment is not the right one for claude-sonnet-5, every candidate must support tool calling, and picking for someone else is how you get an agent quietly answering from a weaker model. Once a model is chosen this is a two-line policy entry plus a check --run to confirm the field lands, so it is cheap to do with that answer in hand.

evidence.detail: nothing built; behaviour, limits and the interaction with Flex come from the fact sheet's fallback section

items.title: Whether agent steps should run at Flex
items.summary: Router's cost-efficient tier is on by default for OpenAI models, which halves cost but puts a tail-latency risk on every agent step; someone has to decide which this app wants.
items.gains: measured -50% on gpt-5.4-mini for identical prompts, and an OpenManus run makes one call per step, so the discount compounds over a run
items.loses: Flex is a different service tier, not a different price for the same service: one measured gpt-5-nano call at Flex took 61 seconds, and OpenManus streams to someone watching a terminal, so a long tail on one step stalls the whole run visibly
items.price: about half, on the Flex-eligible OpenAI ids only; no effect on Claude, which has no tiers on Router
items.why: This is an account-level default rather than something the code asks for, so the migration neither turned it on nor off, and it only matters for OpenAI-model deployments. Both answers are defensible and the app cannot pick: if these runs are batch work from run_flow.py, take the discount; if a person is watching the stream, ROUTER_MIGRATE_SERVICE_TIER=default pins the standard tier on every routed request and costs twice as much. Worth noting that the measured discount is from one model, gpt-5.4-mini, so the saving on whichever model this deployment runs is an assumption, not a number.

evidence.detail: not measured here; the discount, the 61-second outlier and the account default come from the fact sheet's Flex section

items.title: Prompt caching needed no extra work
items.summary: A router.policy.json prompt_cache_key was measured against the plain migration and added nothing, so that branch was deleted rather than shipped.
items.why: An agent loop re-sending its whole history is the textbook case for prompt caching, so I built the policy first and then measured it. On Claude the runtime already sets a cache key from the request label, and that is what produced the caching recorded in m1's evidence: 8,833 of 8,852 input tokens on step 2, against 0 with the label turned off. On OpenAI models the provider caches an identical prefix on its own, with 6,427 of 6,448 tokens cached on step 2 both with the policy and with ROUTER_MIGRATE_POLICY=off. So the lever was already pulled, and shipping the policy would have meant a file to maintain, an extra failure mode in the compiled copy, and a claimed win that two live arms say is not there. Recorded here so nobody spends the afternoon on it again.

evidence.detail: four live calls in two arms per model: claude-haiku-5-5 cached 8,833 of 8,852 with the runtime's label-derived key and 0 of 8,852 with ROUTER_MIGRATE_FEATURE_TAG=off; gpt-6-luna cached 6,427 of 6,448 with the policy and the same 6,427 with ROUTER_MIGRATE_POLICY=off

items.title: The reasoning-model list is also from 2024
items.summary: REASONING_MODELS is ["o1", "o3-mini"], so every current model takes the max_tokens plus temperature branch; the Router path copes, the provider path would not.
items.why: Neither o1 nor o3-mini is active in Router's catalog, so in practice every request takes the else branch and sends max_tokens and temperature. That is fine on Router, where the runtime drops temperature for the 36 ids that reject it (verified live on claude-haiku-5-5, which has temperature: false and returned 200), and it means config.llm.temperature silently stops applying on those models, which m1 records as a loss. Off Router the same request would 400 at the provider. I left it alone rather than extend i1 to this list, because the catalog's reasoning flag is true for most modern models and is not the same question as which parameter name the model wants for its output cap: switching those models to max_completion_tokens would change the request shape for nearly every deployment, including the ones still talking to a vendor endpoint directly. Worth a deliberate fix, separately from the migration.

evidence.detail: a live ask_with_images() call on claude-haiku-5-5 sent temperature 0.0 and returned 200 with a correct answer, so the runtime dropped the field rather than failing the call
